title: The Book Named for His Wife
word: each as a lens for a week
hookLine: a story people tell about a scholar who wrote careful books on schools that disagreed, and named one of them after his wife
carry: one truth, six darshanas: lenses, not team jerseys
tomorrow: Krishna is leaving, and his friend asks to come.

lines: A SCHOLAR BENT OVER HIS BOOK.
THE ONE WHO KEPT THE LAMP LIT.
cards: There's a story people tell about a scholar named Vachaspati Mishra.
He was writing a commentary, and he worked at it so long and so completely that he lost track of everything else, including the woman who kept the lamp lit beside him, his wife.
When he finally looked up and asked who she was, she told him. Moved, so the story goes, he named the book after her: the Bhamati. The story may be legend.
But the scholar's shelf is real, and it's strange. On the last day of this part, it shows how to hold all six darshanas at once.

teach.b: Here's what's strange about the shelf. The Bhamati is a Vedanta commentary, in Shankara's line. But Vachaspati Mishra is also remembered for commentaries on Nyaya, on Samkhya, on Yoga and on Mimamsa.
Schools that argue with each other, sometimes sharply. Among them, a commentary on a book by Mandana Mishra, yesterday's debater.
And he wrote on each of them from the inside, carefully, laying out its case in its own terms. That's what a lens is.

teach.h: A LENS, NOT A TEAM JERSEY.
teach.b: Not a team jersey. A way of seeing you learn well enough to look through. So here are all six, one last time.
Nyaya: how do I know? Vaisheshika: what is this made of? Samkhya: who is watching?
Yoga: what is the mind doing? Mimamsa: what is this act for? Vedanta: what does all of it rest on?
Why can one tradition hold all six?
Many Hindus reach for a line from the Rig Veda: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. It's about the names of the divine, but many teachers read it as the spirit of the six schools too.
That's the teaching to keep: in Hinduism, a darshana is a way of seeing, and one truth can be seen from more than one side. It ends with no winner.
That's the point of the part we're closing, schools of thought, never ranked. The tradition kept all six on one shelf, argued among them for a long time, and kept the lamp lit for the next reader.
Tomorrow the lineage track picks up again, with a different teacher, Krishna speaking to his friend Uddhava in the Bhagavata, on action.

how: Traditional students of Indian philosophy learn the darshanas from their own root texts and commentaries, and classical scholars such as Vachaspati Mishra wrote commentaries on several schools, setting out each one's case in its own terms.

games.q: what does “each as a lens for a week” mean?
o: reading only one commentary on each school
picking one school and defending it like a team
holding all six schools, a day each, none ranked

games.q: the scholar's shelf — tap the pairs.

s: Vachaspati Mishra wrote only on Vedanta
he's remembered for commentaries on Nyaya, Samkhya, Yoga and Mimamsa too.
the story of the Bhamati's name is certain history
it's a story people tell; it may be legend.
the Bhamati is a commentary in Shankara's line of Vedanta
and the same scholar is remembered for commentaries on schools that argue with Vedanta.

games.q: you're a scholar asked to explain a school you don't belong to. what do you do?
o: explain it badly so your own looks better.
lay out its case carefully, in its own terms.
games.why: Vachaspati Mishra is remembered for doing exactly that, for school after school.

practice: Picture the first ordinary thing you'll do tomorrow morning, filling a kettle, finding your keys, opening a door, and let whichever of the six questions arrives first stand in front of it.
Look through it for a few breaths and notice what comes into focus, then set the lens down and rest in the plain scene without any question at all. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight.

wordCard.voice: Each as a lens for a week. The six darshanas, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta, each tried for a day, none of them ranked. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of Vachaspati Mishra's Vedanta commentary, which a story ties to his wife.

carryVoice: Your line: one truth, six darshanas, lenses, not team jerseys. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vachaspati Mishra, Bhamati (on Shankara's Brahma Sutra Bhashya), with his commentaries on Nyaya, Samkhya, Yoga and Mimamsa (including the Nyaya-kanika on Mandana Mishra's Vidhiviveka)
the six darshanas (Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta) as treated earlier in this part of the path
